title: The crimes of ‘The Rings of Power’ against Tolkien
gist: A deputy editor's critical review arguing Amazon Prime's 'The Rings of Power' fails on performances, design and dialogue despite big CGI and soundtrack spending, partly because its writers must dramatise Tolkien's sparse appendices rather than lift lines from the books. He holds up the 1981 BBC radio dramatisation as the best Lord of the Rings adaptation, ahead of Peter Jackson's films.

insights.claim: Alastair Benn argues that the booming soundtracks and vast CGI panoramas of Amazon Prime's 'The Rings of Power' cannot rescue its stale and wooden performances, and expects its third series to repeat the missteps of the first two.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: Spectacle spending does not guarantee quality reception for streaming IP bets; watch critical and audience sentiment around Amazon's costly Tolkien franchise.
insights.quote: Booming soundtracks and vast CGI-generated panoramas cannot rescue the stale and wooden performances that wreck the major set pieces.
insights.locator: Booming soundtracks and vast CGI-generated panoramas

insights.claim: Benn reads attempts in series two of 'The Rings of Power' to imitate the atmosphere of Peter Jackson's films as an implicit admission that series one failed to build something new and distinctive.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: Franchise extensions that drift toward copying the prior hit signal creative weakness and possible diminishing returns on the IP.
insights.quote: an implicit admission of failure to construct something new and special in series one
insights.locator: Booming soundtracks and vast CGI-generated panoramas

insights.claim: The show assigns every character a fixed accent by people of Middle-earth (elves in pompous RP, dwarves broad Scottish, harfoots stage Irish, orcs Cockney, Númenóreans plain RP, men northern English), a choice Benn finds among its most irritating.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: Illustrates the kind of creative decisions that alienate core fan audiences of a premium IP.
insights.locator: One of the more irritating decisions

insights.claim: Amazon's writers are structurally disadvantaged versus the Jackson film writers because the films lifted their most quotable lines directly from the books, whereas 'The Rings of Power' must dramatise events recounted only as dry lists of dates and battles in Tolkien's appendices.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: IP adaptations built on thin source material carry higher creative risk than those mining rich original text; two more series are planned.
insights.quote: They are attempting to dramatise the events drily recounted in a long list of dates and battle names in the appendices
insights.locator: The writers are at a genuine disadvantage

themes.theme: The 1981 BBC radio version as the benchmark

insights.claim: Benn contends the best dramatisation of The Lord of the Rings is not Peter Jackson's films but the BBC's 1981 radio version starring Ian Holm as Frodo, Michael Hordern as Gandalf and John Le Mesurier as Bilbo.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: Lower-budget adaptations faithful to source text can outlast big-budget versions in cultural esteem.
insights.quote: The best dramatisation of The Lord of the Rings is not the films at all, but a radio version produced by the BBC in 1981
insights.locator: The best Lord of the Rings

insights.claim: Benn prizes the BBC radio version for barely altering Tolkien's structure and for its wholly English feel, contrasting it with Jackson's inserted episodes, such as Aragorn being pulled over a cliff by a warg, and the films' transatlantic accents.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: Fidelity to source is a recurring axis of fan judgement for literary franchise adaptations.
